messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Your previous vignette is missing some reported symptoms or demographic details. Rewrite it to include everything.

Previous vignette:
Amir was twenty-seven, a physical therapist at a suburban outpatient clinic, and for three years he had been trying to hold his life together without anyone noticing the cracks. The assault happened when he was twenty-four, about a year after he married Sara. He had gone for a run in the evening along a familiar path near his old apartment. A man he did not know came up from behind, and Amir could still summon the smell of him—a sweet, musky cologne that saturated the air as the man pressed him against a fence. The rest of that evening existed in fragments: the searing pain in his shoulder as he was forced face-down, the sense of his body no longer belonging to him, the moment when something in his mind slipped sideways and he watched it all from above, telling himself this was happening to someone else. That trick of dissociation became his default. Whenever the memory surfaced—and it surfaced constantly—he would automatically shift into a strange, distant calm, as though the whole thing were a story about a stranger. It allowed him to function, but he knew, deep down, that he was using it to disappear from his own life.

At work, Amir was skilled and liked by his patients, but the clinic had become a minefield. Physical therapy required him to place his hands on people’s bodies, to guide their movements, to ask about their pain. He had learned to brace himself every time a patient mentioned a new ache. The word *pain* landed in his chest like a blow, because pain was what he felt during the assault, and now any somatic sensation—a twinge in his own back, a cramp in his leg—sent him into a silent panic. He would check and recheck his body throughout the day, pressing on his ribs, his shoulders, his lower back, scanning for anything that might signal danger or injury. He told himself it was professional vigilance, but he knew it was something else: a constant, exhausting watchfulness that left him drained by noon.

The most difficult triggers were olfactory. A middle-aged man came in for knee rehab wearing a heavy cologne, and Amir’s throat closed. He excused himself, went to the break room, and stood gripping the counter until his breathing steadied. He started avoiding certain hours when he knew that patient would be there, rearranging schedules so he would not have to be in close proximity. Another patient used a scented lotion, and Amir felt a rush of heat, a racing heart, an urge to flee. He began to dread the start of each shift, hypervigilant to the smells that drifted through the clinic.

The startle responses had grown worse over time. If a patient reached out unexpectedly to touch his arm during a conversation, Amir would flinch, sometimes yanking his hand away. He could see the confusion on their faces, and he would mumble an apology, claiming he was just startled by the suddenness. Sudden movements in his peripheral vision—a colleague walking quickly past, a door swinging open—triggered the same jolt of alarm, as if his body believed danger was imminent. The world felt full of ambushes. He could not relax, even at home. Sara would come up behind him to hug him, and he would stiffen, his heart hammering. He saw the hurt in her eyes, but he could not explain it. He told himself she would not understand, and besides, he could not find the words for what had happened. He had never told her the full story.

Intimacy with Sara had become nearly impossible. Any sexual situation, even a kiss that lingered too long, brought him back to the assault. He would go distant, his mind detaching, pretending it was not his body being touched. Sara noticed his withdrawal, and she asked gently if something was wrong. He said he was just tired. He could see their marriage fraying along a seam he did not know how to mend. He felt a deep, corroding shame about his body—the body that had been used, that had not fought back, that now seemed permanently marked. He had come to believe he could never trust himself again; he had failed to protect himself that evening, and so he could not rely on his own instincts now. He also believed his emotions were broken for good. Occasionally he cried in the shower, but mostly he felt nothing—a hollowed-out numbness that scared him more than the fear did.

What finally brought him to therapy was a session with a patient who had a chronic shoulder condition. The patient mentioned "the pain was so bad that night," and Amir’s mind flashed to the fence, to the gravel digging into his cheek. He dissociated mid-sentence, fumbled an exercise instruction, and walked out of the room. His supervisor noticed and expressed concern. That night, Sara told him she could not keep living with someone who was not really there. She said she loved him, but she felt alone. The next morning, Amir called a clinic that specialised in trauma. He was terrified that talking about it would shatter what little composure he had left—but he was more afraid of losing Sara, and of spending the rest of his life pretending that what happened to his body had happened to someone else.

Missing items that MUST appear in the rewrite:
MISSING FROM VIGNETTE:
- Avoid Thinking: The vignette does not describe the patient actively avoiding thinking about the event; instead, it describes dissociation as a response to memories.

---

Rewrite the full vignette (4–5 paragraphs, third person) incorporating all missing items as lived clinical experience.
Preserve all content from the previous vignette that was already correct — only add what is missing.
Do not use section headers or bullet points.
